questions.decision: One of the two assistant prompts contained ~97% of the brief pasted verbatim â€” a one-shot delegation of the whole task rather than a decomposed plan
questions.question: Walk me through how you turned the brief into your first working step. Before you wrote or generated any code, what did you decide the task actually broke down into, and which part did you deliberately do first â€” and why that part?
questions.listenFor: A concrete decomposition they can reconstruct unprompted (e.g. 'first I had to understand the flush cycle, so I traced X before touching Y'), named files or functions they read first, and a reason the ordering mattered for this codebase specifically.
questions.redFlag: Describes the final artifact instead of the process, or gives a generic waterfall ('first I read the requirements, then I implemented') with no repo-specific anchor; cannot say what they did before the first generation.

questions.decision: The tooling trace shows iteration depth 2 â€” a second prompt followed the initial one-shot delegation
questions.question: Your first pass with the assistant wasn't your last â€” something made you go back a second time. What specifically was wrong or missing in the first output, how did you notice it, and what did you change in how you asked?
questions.listenFor: A specific defect they can name (a broken behavior, a missed constraint, a wrong assumption in the generated code), how they detected it (ran it, read it, diffed it), and a concrete reformulation of the follow-up.
questions.redFlag: Claims the first output was basically fine and the second prompt was cosmetic, or can't recall what the correction was about â€” a genuine author remembers what forced the second round.

questions.decision: The brief's 'feel safe' requirement admits several distinct loss modes (unflushed edits on reload, closed-tab loss, stale restore); the submission committed to an interpretation without recorded deliberation
questions.question: The brief asked that the editing experience 'feel safe.' There are at least three different ways a user can lose work here. Which loss scenario did you decide your solution actually covers, which one did you consciously leave uncovered, and what would have to be true about the users for you to flip that choice?
questions.listenFor: They can enumerate the loss modes in their own words, name the one they scoped out and the cost of covering it (e.g. local-draft reconciliation conflicts, beforeunload UX), and give a plausible counterfactual condition.
questions.redFlag: Treats 'safe' as a single obvious feature, defends whatever shipped as covering everything, or discovers the uncovered loss mode live for the first time during the question.

questions.decision: The submission sits on top of an existing flush()/re-buffer pipeline whose event log has an append-only hash-chain integrity contract; the trace shows little evidence of reading before generating
questions.question: The session event log in this codebase has an ordering and integrity contract on the server side. Open the flush path with me: talk me through what the existing code guarantees about event order and what a change like yours could break in it. What did you check before deciding your change was compatible?
questions.listenFor: Recognizes on sight what re-buffering does on a failed flush, articulates why appending out of order or replaying a batch corrupts the chain, and can point to the specific thing they verified (or honestly names that they didn't and reasons about it well live).
questions.redFlag: Reads the code aloud without interpretation, is surprised the hash chain exists, or asserts compatibility without being able to say what property they were preserving.

questions.question: Suppose a flush fails, the events get re-buffered, and the next flush succeeds â€” what does the server see? Tell me how you convinced yourself, before submitting, that this exact retry path doesn't double-append the batch, and what you would run right now to prove it either way.
questions.listenFor: Either a concrete test or manual drill they actually performed (with what they observed), or an honest 'I didn't test that' followed by immediately designing a sharp check â€” naming where the dedup or idempotency would have to live.
questions.redFlag: Insists it works because the happy path worked, hand-waves 'the framework handles retries,' or proposes a verification that only re-exercises the success path.
